title: Sharabhanga waits for Rama
hookLine: an old sage makes heaven wait for one look at Rama, which is why Hindus still line up for darshan
carry: darshan: one sight of god outweighs heaven
last: THE SELF WAS NEVER THE MONSTER.

cards: Rama follows Viradha's directions, and near Sharabhanga's hermitage he stops. There's a chariot in the air above the clearing, blazing like the sun, pulled by green horses.
A white umbrella shades the figure in it, and attendants crowd around. That's Indra, Rama tells Lakshmana, king of the gods, talking with the sage.
And as the brothers walk closer, Indra says something to his companions, and the chariot rises and goes.

teach.b: Why does Indra leave? Valmiki gives his reason: Rama has a great task ahead, and Indra will meet him only once it's done. The text hints at a war the gods need Rama to fight, but says no more.
Picture it anyway: the king of the gods stepping aside for a man in bark clothes.
Rama goes in, and the very old sage welcomes him. Indra came to take me to Brahma's world, Sharabhanga says. I've earned it by my tapas.
But I heard you were near, and I wouldn't go until I had seen you, my guest. Think about that. Heaven is waiting at the door, and he makes it wait, for one look at Rama.

teach.h: DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.
teach.b: For devotees, Rama is Vishnu himself, and this is darshan: seeing God, and being seen. It's why Hindus go to the temple even with a shrine at home.
You stand in line, the curtain opens, and for a few seconds you look at the murti and the murti looks back at you. Many say that moment is the point of the whole visit.
Then the sage offers Rama all the worlds his tapas has won. Rama declines, kindly. I'll earn my own worlds.
Just tell me where to live. Sharabhanga points him to another sage, Sutikshna. But first he asks Rama to stay and watch.
He has one last thing to do.

how: In the text, Indra withdraws before meeting Rama, and some devotees read the scene as the gods waiting on Rama's mission.

o: the king of the gods who visits in a blazing chariot
the old sage who waits to see Rama and offers him his merit
a forest giant who guards the way to a sage's hut

games.q: at Sharabhanga's hermitage — tap the pairs.

s: darshan means praying with your eyes closed
it means seeing God in the murti, and being seen. Sharabhanga made heaven wait for it.
Sharabhanga delays going to Brahma's world to see Rama
he wouldn't leave until he had seen his guest.
he declines and asks only where he should live.

games.q: Sharabhanga has earned Brahma's world, and Indra has come to take him. what does he do?
o: go at once; heaven doesn't wait.
make heaven wait until he has seen Rama.
send Indra to fetch Rama first.
games.why: he waits for one look at Rama. that's darshan, the sight Hindus still line up for at the temple.

practice: Hindus can take darshan in the mind, too. Close your eyes and picture the face of the form of God you know best, Rama, Krishna, Ganesha, the Goddess, the way it looks when the temple curtain opens.
If you pray, just look, and let yourself be looked at, as you breathe. If you don't, picture a face that has looked at you with love, and rest in being seen.

wordCard.voice: Sharabhanga. The old sage who made heaven wait so he could see Rama, then offered him all his merit, which Rama kindly declined.

orig.note: Sanskrit śarabhaṅga: the name of the old sage of Dandaka who waits to see Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: darshan: one sight of God outweighs heaven. Sharabhanga made heaven wait for it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 5 (Indra at the hermitage; Sharabhanga's offer; Rama's answer)
